title: Τὸ κρήδεμνον
titleEn: The Storm and the Veil — Odyssey 5.291–387
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Poseidon gathers the clouds, stirs up the sea with his trident and sets all four winds blowing at once. Odysseus, his strength failing, wishes he had died at Troy, where he would at least have had burial and fame, and at once a great wave throws him from his raft, a squall snaps the mast, and he is held under, weighed down by the clothes Calypso gave him, though he struggles back aboard. The sea-goddess Ino, called Leucothea, once a mortal woman, pities him: rising from the sea like a bird, she tells him to strip, abandon the raft and swim for the land of the Phaeacians, and gives him her deathless head-veil to bind beneath his chest, to be thrown back into the sea when he reaches land. Odysseus suspects a trick and resolves to stay with the raft while it holds, until another wave from Poseidon scatters its timbers; then he rides a single beam, strips, binds on the veil and dives in. Poseidon, content that Odysseus will suffer enough, drives off to his home at Aegae, and Athena stills every wind but the North Wind, which carries Odysseus on toward the Phaeacians.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν σύναγεν νεφέλας, ἐτάραξε δὲ πόντον
χερσὶ τρίαιναν ἑλών·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn synagen nephelas, etaraxe de ponton
chersi triainan helōn·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he gathered the clouds, and stirred up the open-sea,
his trident taking in his hands;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and gathered the clouds and stirred up the sea, taking his trident in his hands;
sentences.n: The speaker is Poseidon, whose words to himself closed the previous part. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is the participial form of the speech-closing formula. σύναγεν is the imperfect of συνάγω ‘bring together’ without its augment (Attic συνῆγεν): Homer’s past tenses may drop the ἐ-, and this part is full of them. ἐτάραξε is the aorist of ταράσσω ‘stir up’. τρίαινα is the three-pronged spear that is Poseidon’s own weapon, and ἑλών, the aorist participle of αἱρέω, is ‘having taken’. Gathering clouds is the work that gives Zeus his title νεφεληγερέτα; here the sea-god does it.

sentences.t:
πάσας δ’ ὀρόθυνεν ἀέλλας
παντοίων ἀνέμων, σὺν δὲ νεφέεσσι κάλυψε
γαῖαν ὁμοῦ καὶ πόντον·
sentences.tr:
pasas d’ orothynen aellas
pantoiōn anemōn, syn de nepheessi kalypse
gaian homou kai ponton·
sentences.i: he roused all the blasts of every kind of wind, and with clouds he hid land and sea alike;
sentences.n: ὀρόθυνεν is the unaugmented aorist of ὀροθύνω ‘stir up, rouse’. ἄελλα is a ‘blast, gust’, and παντοίων ἀνέμων ‘of winds of every kind’ depends on it. νεφέεσσι, from νέφος, is the first of this part’s long datives in -εσσι; the -οισι and -ῃσι datives are just as common. σύν can be taken as an adverb, ‘together’, or with κάλυψε by tmesis, the preverb standing apart from its verb: συνεκάλυψε ‘covered up’. γαῖαν ὁμοῦ καὶ πόντον is ‘earth and sea alike’.

sentences.t: ὀρώρει δ’ οὐρανόθεν νύξ.
sentences.tr: orōrei d’ ouranothen nyx.
sentences.l: and night had sprung up from the sky.
sentences.i: and night had sprung up out of the sky.
sentences.n: ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse; (intransitive) arise, spring up’, without augment: night ‘had sprung up’ and was upon them. οὐρανόθεν has the suffix -θεν ‘from’, ‘from the sky’; -θεν, -θι and -δε mark place from, place where and place to. The darkness is the storm-cloud’s, not nightfall: the clouds of 293 have shut out the light in the middle of the voyage.

sentences.t:
σὺν δ’ Εὖρός τε Νότος τ’ ἔπεσον Ζέφυρός τε δυσαὴς
καὶ Βορέης αἰθρηγενέτης, μέγα κῦμα κυλίνδων.
sentences.tr:
syn d’ Euros te Notos t’ epeson Zephyros te dysaēs
kai Boreēs aithrēgenetēs, mega kyma kylindōn.
sentences.l:
And together the East Wind and the South Wind fell on, and the ill-blowing West Wind,
and the North Wind born of the clear air, rolling a great wave.
sentences.i: The East Wind and the South Wind clashed together, and the ill-blowing West Wind, and the North Wind born of the clear air, rolling up a great wave.
sentences.n: σὺν … ἔπεσον is tmesis for συνέπεσον ‘fell together, clashed’, an aorist of συμπίπτω; this one keeps its augment, beside the unaugmented πέσε of 315. All four winds blow at once. δυσαής is ‘ill-blowing’, from δυσ- ‘bad’ and ἄημι ‘blow’. Βορέης is the Ionic form of Βορέας. αἰθρηγενέτης is disputed: ‘born of the clear upper air’ (αἴθρη) is followed here, but it can also be taken actively, ‘bringing clear skies’, as the north wind does in Greece. The participle κυλίνδων agrees with Βορέης alone.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότ’ Ὀδυσσῆος λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ,
ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
kai tot’ Odyssēos lyto gounata kai philon ētor,
ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l:
And then Odysseus’ knees were loosed, and his dear heart,
and, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And then Odysseus’ knees gave way, and his heart too, and, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: λύτο, ‘were loosed’, is an unaugmented root aorist middle of λύω. γούνατα is the epic plural of γόνυ ‘knee’ (Attic γόνατα). Loosened knees are Homer’s picture of strength failing from fear or shock; the same words were used of Penelope at 4.703. φίλον ἦτορ is little more than ‘his own heart’. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed, troubled’. In ὃν … θυμόν, ὅς is the possessive ‘his own’, easily mistaken for the relative. μεγαλήτορα keeps the house ‘great-spirited’. The line introduces a speech to himself.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγὼ δειλός, τί νύ μοι μήκιστα γένηται;
sentences.tr: ō moi egō deilos, ti ny moi mēkista genētai;
sentences.l: “Oh me, I, miserable one, what now will happen to me in the end?
sentences.i: “Oh me, miserable that I am, what is to become of me in the end?
sentences.n: ὤ μοι is a cry of distress, ‘oh me!’, with μοι a dative of the person affected. ἐγὼ δειλός, in the nominative, is part of the cry: ‘I, miserable one’. δειλός is ‘wretched, miserable’, and in other contexts ‘cowardly’. γένηται is an aorist subjunctive in a question of doubt, ‘what is to happen?’. μήκιστα, a superlative adverb of μακρός ‘long’, is here ‘at the last, in the end’. νυ is a weak ‘now, then’.

sentences.t:
δείδω μὴ δὴ πάντα θεὰ νημερτέα εἶπεν,
ἥ μ’ ἔφατ’ ἐν πόντῳ, πρὶν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι,
ἄλγε’ ἀναπλήσειν· τὰ δὲ δὴ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται.
sentences.tr:
deidō mē dē panta thea nēmertea eipen,
hē m’ ephat’ en pontōi, prin patrida gaian hikesthai,
alge’ anaplēsein· ta de dē nyn panta teleitai.
sentences.l:
I fear that the goddess spoke all things unerring,
who said that I, on the open-sea, before reaching my fatherland,
would fill up my pains; and now indeed all these things are being fulfilled.
sentences.i: I fear that all the goddess said was unerring, she who told me I would fill up my pains to the full out on the sea, before ever I reached my fatherland; and now, indeed, all of it is coming to pass.
sentences.n: δείδω is the epic form of δέδοικα ‘I fear’. μή with the aorist indicative εἶπεν fears something already done. νημερτέα is uncontracted (Attic νημερτῆ), ‘unerring’. θεά is Calypso: ἀναπλήσειν, the future infinitive of ἀναπίμπλημι ‘fill up’, as one fills a measure, recalls her κήδε’ ἀναπλῆσαι at 5.207, with ἄλγε’ (= ἄλγεα) ‘pains’ for κήδεα ‘sorrows’; ἐν πόντῳ is his own addition. τελεῖται is present passive, ‘is being fulfilled’: the prophecy comes true as he speaks. The last half-line is word for word 2.176 and keeps its English there.

sentences.t:
οἵοισιν νεφέεσσι περιστέφει οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν
Ζεύς, ἐτάραξε δὲ πόντον, ἐπισπέρχουσι δ’ ἄελλαι
παντοίων ἀνέμων.
sentences.tr:
hoioisin nepheessi peristephei ouranon euryn
Zeus, etaraxe de ponton, episperchousi d’ aellai
pantoiōn anemōn.
sentences.l:
With what clouds he wreathes round the wide sky,
Zeus, and he has stirred up the open-sea, and the blasts press on
of winds of every kind.
sentences.i: With what clouds Zeus is wreathing the wide sky! He has stirred up the sea, and the blasts of every kind of wind press on.
sentences.n: οἵοισιν, an exclamatory relative with the dative in -οισι, is ‘with what (clouds)!’, and νεφέεσσι has the dative -εσσι. περιστέφει is ‘wreathes round, crowns’. Odysseus names Ζεύς, held over to the head of 304, as the maker of the storm; the reader knows from 291–296 that it was Poseidon. ἐτάραξε δὲ πόντον repeats the narrator’s words at 291, and ἄελλαι παντοίων ἀνέμων those of 292–293. ἐπισπέρχουσι is ‘drive on, press hard’.

sentences.t: νῦν μοι σῶς αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος.
sentences.tr: nyn moi sōs aipys olethros.
sentences.l: Now for me steep destruction is sure.
sentences.i: Now my steep destruction is certain.
sentences.n: The verb ‘is’ is left out, as often in Homer. σῶς, usually ‘safe, sound’, here means ‘sure, certain’: his destruction is secure. αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος keeps the house ‘steep destruction’, the formula of 1.11 and 1.37; the usual explanation of αἰπύς ‘steep, sheer’ is that ruin is pictured as a fall from a height. μοι is a dative of the person concerned, ‘for me’.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μάκαρες Δαναοὶ καὶ τετράκις, οἳ τότ’ ὄλοντο
Τροίῃ ἐν εὐρείῃ χάριν Ἀτρεΐδῃσι φέροντες.
sentences.tr:
tris makares Danaoi kai tetrakis, hoi tot’ olonto
Troiēi en eureiēi charin Atreïdēisi pherontes.
sentences.l:
Three times blessed the Danaans, and four times, who perished then
in Troy the broad, bringing favour to the sons of Atreus.
sentences.i: Three times blessed were the Danaans, and four times over, who perished then in the broad land of Troy, doing a kindness to the sons of Atreus.
sentences.n: τρὶς … καὶ τετράκις ‘three times and four times’ heightens μάκαρες ‘blessed, fortunate’, the word used of the gods. Δαναοί is one of Homer’s three names for the Greeks, with Ἀχαιοί and Ἀργεῖοι. ὄλοντο is the unaugmented aorist of ὄλλυμαι ‘perish’. Τροίῃ has Ionic η where Attic has long α, and Ἀτρεΐδῃσι the dative plural in -ῃσι. χάριν φέροντες is ‘bringing a favour’, doing a service: they fought for the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὴ ἐγώ γ’ ὄφελον θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε μοι πλεῖστοι χαλκήρεα δοῦρα
Τρῶες ἐπέρριψαν περὶ Πηλεΐωνι θανόντι.
sentences.tr:
hōs dē egō g’ ophelon thaneein kai potmon epispein
ēmati tōi hote moi pleistoi chalkērea doura
Trōes eperripsan peri Pēleïōni thanonti.
sentences.l:
Would that I too had died and met my fate
on that day when at me, in their greatest numbers, bronze-fitted spears
the Trojans hurled, around the son of Peleus, dead.
sentences.i: If only I too had died and met my fate on that day when the Trojans in their greatest numbers hurled their bronze-fitted spears at me around the dead son of Peleus.
sentences.n: ὡς … ὄφελον with the infinitive is a wish that can no longer come true, ‘would that I had’; ὄφελον is the unaugmented aorist of ὀφείλω ‘owe, ought’. θανέειν is an uncontracted aorist infinitive (Attic θανεῖν). πότμον ἐπισπεῖν, ‘to meet one’s fate’, has the English it has at 4.562. χαλκήρεα is ‘fitted with bronze’, of the spear-heads. περὶ Πηλεΐωνι θανόντι is ‘round the dead son of Peleus’, that is Achilles, over whose body the fight went on; Odysseus names him only by his father.

sentences.t: τῷ κ’ ἔλαχον κτερέων, καί μευ κλέος ἦγον Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.tr: tōi k’ elachon ktereōn, kai meu kleos ēgon Achaioi·
sentences.l: Then I would have got my share of funeral-honours, and the Achaeans would be carrying my fame abroad;
sentences.i: Then I would have had my due of funeral honours, and the Achaeans would be carrying my fame abroad;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘in that case, then’. κ’ is κε, the epic equivalent of ἄν, and with the past indicatives ἔλαχον and ἦγον it marks what would have happened and did not. ἔλαχον, an aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’, takes the genitive κτερέων ‘funeral honours’, the gifts and rites paid to the dead. μευ is an epic genitive of ἐγώ (Attic μου). κλέος ἄγειν is to carry a man’s fame abroad; the imperfect ἦγον pictures it still going on.

sentences.t: νῦν δέ με λευγαλέῳ θανάτῳ εἵμαρτο ἁλῶναι.
sentences.tr: nyn de me leugaleōi thanatōi heimarto halōnai.
sentences.l: But now it was allotted for me to be caught by a pitiful death.”
sentences.i: But as it is, it was my lot to be caught by a pitiful death.”
sentences.n: εἵμαρτο is the pluperfect of μείρομαι ‘receive a share’, used impersonally: ‘it had been allotted’, that is, fated. The same root gives μοῖρα and μόρος. ἁλῶναι is the aorist infinitive of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be caught, taken’, and λευγαλέῳ θανάτῳ is the means: death takes him like a prey. λευγαλέος is ‘pitiful, sorry’. A death at sea leaves no body for the rites and no fame, and that is the point of the contrast with 311.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα μιν εἰπόντ’ ἔλασεν μέγα κῦμα κατ’ ἄκρης
δεινὸν ἐπεσσύμενον, περὶ δὲ σχεδίην ἐλέλιξε.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara min eipont’ elasen mega kyma kat’ akrēs
deinon epessymenon, peri de schediēn elelixe.
sentences.l:
As he said this, then, a great wave drove at him from on high,
dread, rushing on, and whirled the raft around.
sentences.i: As he said this, a great wave crashed down on him from above, dread and rushing on, and spun the raft about.
sentences.n: μιν εἰπόντ’ is ‘him, as he spoke’: εἰπόντ’ is εἰπόντα, elided, agreeing with μιν, the epic accusative pronoun (Attic αὐτόν). ἔλασεν is the unaugmented aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive; strike’. κατ’ ἄκρης is ‘down from the top’, of a wave breaking from its crest. δεινόν ‘dread’ agrees with κῦμα, though it can also be taken as an adverb. ἐπεσσύμενον is the perfect participle of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush upon’. In περὶ … ἐλέλιξε, aorist of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl’, περί is an adverb, ‘round about’, or stands apart from its verb by tmesis.

sentences.t:
τῆλε δ’ ἀπὸ σχεδίης αὐτὸς πέσε, πηδάλιον δὲ
ἐκ χειρῶν προέηκε·
sentences.tr:
tēle d’ apo schediēs autos pese, pēdalion de
ek cheirōn proeēke·
sentences.l:
Far from the raft he himself fell, and the steering-oar
out of his hands he let go;
sentences.i: He himself fell far from the raft, and he let the steering-oar slip from his hands;
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘he himself’ is set against the raft: the man is thrown one way and the craft goes another. πέσε is the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω (Attic ἔπεσε). πηδάλιον is the steering-oar he made at 255. προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι ‘let go forward, let fall’: the oar is swept out of his grip. The ano teleia closes the clause, and the damage to the craft follows.

sentences.t:
μέσον δέ οἱ ἱστὸν ἔαξεν
δεινὴ μισγομένων ἀνέμων ἐλθοῦσα θύελλα,
τηλοῦ δὲ σπεῖρον καὶ ἐπίκριον ἔμπεσε πόντῳ.
sentences.tr:
meson de hoi histon eaxen
deinē misgomenōn anemōn elthousa thyella,
tēlou de speiron kai epikrion empese pontōi.
sentences.l:
and in the middle his mast was snapped
by a dread storm-blast of mingling winds that came upon it,
and far off sail and yard fell into the open-sea.
sentences.i: and a dread storm-blast of mingling winds came on and snapped his mast in the middle, and sail and yard fell far off into the sea.
sentences.n: ἔαξεν is the aorist of ἄγνυμι ‘break, snap’, with the syllabic augment ἐ- that verbs once beginning with ϝ take. μέσον is predicative: the mast broke ‘in the middle’. οἱ is ‘his’, a dative of the person affected. μισγομένων ἀνέμων is ‘of winds mingling’, the four winds of 295–296 meeting. θύελλα is a ‘storm-blast, squall’. σπεῖρον is a woven cloth, here the sail; ἐπίκριον is the yard of 254. ἔμπεσε is the unaugmented aorist of ἐμπίπτω, with the dative πόντῳ.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόβρυχα θῆκε πολὺν χρόνον, οὐδ’ ἐδυνάσθη
αἶψα μάλ’ ἀνσχεθέειν μεγάλου ὑπὸ κύματος ὁρμῆς·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ar’ hypobrycha thēke polyn chronon, oud’ edynasthē
aipsa mal’ anschetheein megalou hypo kymatos hormēs·
sentences.l:
And him it set under water a long time, nor was he able
very quickly to rise up from under the great wave’s onrush;
sentences.i: It kept him under water a long time, and he could not come up quickly from beneath the onrush of the great wave;
sentences.n: The subject of θῆκε is not stated; it is the wave, or the storm. ὑπόβρυχα ‘under water’ is used predicatively with θῆκε ‘put, set’: ‘set him under water’. ἐδυνάσθη is a passive-form aorist of δύναμαι ‘be able’. ἀνσχεθέειν is an aorist infinitive of ἀνέχω from the stem σχεθ-, with ἀν- for ἀνα- and the epic ending -έειν: ‘hold himself up, come to the surface’. ὑπό with the genitive ὁρμῆς is ‘from under the rush’.

sentences.t: εἵματα γάρ ῥ’ ἐβάρυνε, τά οἱ πόρε δῖα Καλυψώ.
sentences.tr: heimata gar rh’ ebaryne, ta hoi pore dia Kalypsō.
sentences.l: for the clothes weighed him down, which heavenly Calypso had given him.
sentences.i: for he was weighed down by the clothes which heavenly Calypso had given him.
sentences.n: ῥ’ is ῥα, a worn-down ἄρα. ἐβάρυνε is the aorist of βαρύνω ‘weigh down’, with the clothes as subject and ‘him’ understood. τά is the article-form used as a relative, ‘which’. πόρε, the unaugmented aorist ἔπορον ‘gave, furnished’, has no present in use. οἱ is ‘to him’. δῖα Καλυψώ keeps the house ‘heavenly Calypso’. These are the fragrant clothes she put on him at 264, and the goddess’s gift now drags him under.

sentences.t:
ὀψὲ δὲ δή ῥ’ ἀνέδυ, στόματος δ’ ἐξέπτυσεν ἅλμην
πικρήν, ἥ οἱ πολλὴ ἀπὸ κρατὸς κελάρυζεν.
sentences.tr:
opse de dē rh’ anedy, stomatos d’ exeptysen halmēn
pikrēn, hē hoi pollē apo kratos kelaryzen.
sentences.l:
But late, at last, he came up, and from his mouth spat out the salt water,
bitter, which in plenty from his head ran gurgling down.
sentences.i: At long last he came up, and spat the bitter salt water from his mouth, while it streamed down plentifully from his head, gurgling.
sentences.n: ὀψὲ δὲ δή is ‘but only late, at last’. ἀνέδυ is the root aorist of ἀναδύομαι ‘come up, emerge’. στόματος is a genitive of separation, ‘out of his mouth’. ἅλμη is ‘salt water, brine’, and πικρήν, with Ionic η, runs over into 323. κρατός is a genitive of κάρη ‘head’. κελάρυζεν is the unaugmented imperfect of κελαρύζω, a word that imitates the sound of running water: ‘gurgled, babbled’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὣς σχεδίης ἐπελήθετο, τειρόμενός περ,
ἀλλὰ μεθορμηθεὶς ἐνὶ κύμασιν ἐλλάβετ’ αὐτῆς,
ἐν μέσσῃ δὲ καθῖζε τέλος θανάτου ἀλεείνων.
sentences.tr:
all’ oud’ hōs schediēs epelētheto, teiromenos per,
alla methormētheis eni kymasin ellabet’ autēs,
en messēi de kathize telos thanatou aleeinōn.
sentences.l:
But not even so did he forget the raft, worn down though he was,
but, darting after it among the waves, he caught hold of it,
and in the middle of it he sat, the end of death avoiding.
sentences.i: Yet even so, worn out as he was, he did not forget the raft, but lunged after it through the waves and caught hold of it, and sat down in the middle of it, shunning the end that death brings.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὥς is ‘but not even so’, the phrase of 1.6. ἐπελήθετο, with the genitive σχεδίης, is ‘forgot’. τειρόμενός περ has concessive περ, ‘worn though he was’, where Attic would use καίπερ. μεθορμηθείς is ‘darting after’, μετα- with ὁρμάω. ἐλλάβετ’, with the λ doubled, is ἐλάβετο ‘took hold of’, again with the genitive. μέσσῃ is epic for μέσῃ. τέλος θανάτου, ‘the end of death’, is death as the end that completes a life. ἀλεείνων is ‘shunning’.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἐφόρει μέγα κῦμα κατὰ ῥόον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ephorei mega kyma kata rhoon entha kai entha.
sentences.l: And it the great wave carried along the current, here and there.
sentences.i: And the great wave carried the raft this way and that along the current.
sentences.n: τήν is the pronoun ‘it’, the raft, feminine like σχεδίη. ἐφόρει is the imperfect of φορέω, a frequentative of φέρω: ‘kept carrying’. κατὰ ῥόον is ‘along the current, with the stream’; the sea is pictured as flowing. ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα, ‘here and there’, returns at the end of 330, where the simile that follows applies it.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ὀπωρινὸς Βορέης φορέῃσιν ἀκάνθας
ἂμ πεδίον, πυκιναὶ δὲ πρὸς ἀλλήλῃσιν ἔχονται,
ὣς τὴν ἂμ πέλαγος ἄνεμοι φέρον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ opōrinos Boreēs phoreēisin akanthas
am pedion, pykinai de pros allēlēisin echontai,
hōs tēn am pelagos anemoi pheron entha kai entha·
sentences.i: As when the late-summer North Wind carries thistles over the plain, and they cling close-packed to one another, so the winds carried the raft this way and that over the open sea;
sentences.n: A simile opened by ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ‘and as when’ and closed by ὥς ‘so’ at 330. ὀπωρινός is from ὀπώρα, the season at the end of summer when fruit ripens. φορέῃσιν is a subjunctive with the epic ending -ῃσι, as usual in a simile. ἄκανθαι are thistles or thorny plants, dried and bowled along in tangled clumps. ἀλλήλῃσιν has the dative -ῃσι. ἂμ is ἀνά cut short before a labial, ‘over, across’. πέλαγος is the open sea, the high water.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοτε μέν τε Νότος Βορέῃ προβάλεσκε φέρεσθαι,
ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτ’ Εὖρος Ζεφύρῳ εἴξασκε διώκειν.
sentences.tr:
allote men te Notos Boreēi probaleske pheresthai,
allote d’ aut’ Euros Zephyrōi eixaske diōkein.
sentences.l:
At one time the South Wind would toss it to the North Wind to carry,
at another, again, the East Wind would yield it to the West Wind to chase.
sentences.i: At times the South Wind would toss it over to the North Wind to be carried, at times the East Wind would give it up to the West Wind to chase.
sentences.n: προβάλεσκε and εἴξασκε are iterative forms in -σκ-, without augment: ‘kept tossing’, ‘kept yielding’. The suffix marks an action done over and over. ἄλλοτε μέν … ἄλλοτε δ’ is ‘at one time … at another’, and τε is the epic τε of what happens again and again. φέρεσθαι and διώκειν are infinitives of purpose. The four winds of 295–296 pass the raft from one to another.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ἴδεν Κάδμου θυγάτηρ, καλλίσφυρος Ἰνώ,
Λευκοθέη, ἣ πρὶν μὲν ἔην βροτὸς αὐδήεσσα,
νῦν δ’ ἁλὸς ἐν πελάγεσσι θεῶν ἒξ ἔμμορε τιμῆς.
sentences.tr:
ton de iden Kadmou thygatēr, kallisphyros Inō,
Leukotheē, hē prin men eēn brotos audēessa,
nyn d’ halos en pelagessi theōn ex emmore timēs.
sentences.l:
But him saw the daughter of Cadmus, fair-ankled Ino,
Leucothea, who before was a mortal endowed with speech,
but now in the salt-sea’s open waters has her portion of honour from the gods.
sentences.i: But the daughter of Cadmus saw him, fair-ankled Ino, Leucothea, who was once a mortal, speaking with a human voice, but now in the open waters of the salt sea has her portion of honour from the gods.
sentences.n: ἴδεν is unaugmented. Cadmus was the founder of Thebes. καλλίσφυρος is ‘fair-ankled’, from σφυρόν ‘ankle’. Λευκοθέη, ‘White Goddess’, is her name as a goddess of the sea. αὐδήεσσα is from αὐδή ‘voice, speech’, ‘endowed with speech’; the ancient explanation, ‘speaking with a human voice’, as against the gods’ speech, is followed in the English, but the word’s exact force is debated. ἔην is ἦν. πελάγεσσι has the dative -εσσι. θεῶν ἒξ is ἐκ θεῶν, the preposition placed after its noun and accented. ἔμμορε, a perfect of μείρομαι, is ‘has a share of’, with the genitive τιμῆς.

sentences.t:
ἥ ῥ’ Ὀδυσῆ’ ἐλέησεν ἀλώμενον, ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα,
αἰθυίῃ δ’ ἐικυῖα ποτῇ ἀνεδύσετο λίμνης,
ἷζε δ’ ἐπὶ σχεδίης πολυδέσμου εἶπέ τε μῦθον·
sentences.tr:
hē rh’ Odysē’ eleēsen alōmenon, alge’ echonta,
aithuiēi d’ eikuia potēi anedyseto limnēs,
hize d’ epi schediēs polydesmou eipe te mython·
sentences.l:
She then pitied Odysseus as he wandered, having pains,
and, like to a shearwater in flight, rose up from the water,
and sat upon the raft of many bonds and uttered a speech:
sentences.i: She pitied Odysseus as he wandered, beset by pains, and rose up from the water like a shearwater in flight, and sat on the raft of many lashings, and spoke:
sentences.n: Ὀδυσῆ’ is Ὀδυσῆα, elided. ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα is ‘having pains’. αἴθυια is a sea-bird whose kind is not known; shearwater, gull and diver have all been proposed. ἐικυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’. ποτῇ is taken as the dative of ποτή ‘flight’. ἀνεδύσετο is an aorist of ἀναδύομαι with -σ- and thematic endings. λίμνη, standing water, is here the sea. σχεδίη πολύδεσμος keeps the house ‘raft of many bonds’. εἶπέ τε μῦθον introduces the speech; μῦθος is a thing said.

sentences.t:
κάμμορε, τίπτε τοι ὧδε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων
ὠδύσατ’ ἐκπάγλως, ὅτι τοι κακὰ πολλὰ φυτεύει;
sentences.tr:
kammore, tipte toi hōde Poseidaōn enosichthōn
ōdysat’ ekpaglōs, hoti toi kaka polla phyteuei;
sentences.l:
“Ill-fated one, why has Poseidon the earth-shaker so
come-to-hate you, terribly, that he plants many evils for you?
sentences.i: “Ill-fated man, why has Poseidon the earth-shaker come to hate you so terribly, that he is planting many evils for you?
sentences.n: κάμμορε keeps the house ‘Ill-fated one’; it is κατάμορε, built on μόρος ‘portion’, with κατα- cut short and its τ assimilated. τίπτε is ‘why?’, from τί ποτε. ὠδύσατ’ is ὠδύσατο, the aorist of ὀδύσσομαι ‘hate’, which puns on the hero’s name as at 1.62. ἐκπάγλως is ‘terribly, vehemently’. ὅτι is ‘that’, giving the result. φυτεύει is ‘plants’: the evils are sown like a crop. τοι is σοι.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν δή σε καταφθίσει μάλα περ μενεαίνων.
sentences.tr: ou men dē se kataphthisei mala per meneainōn.
sentences.l: Yet surely he will not destroy you, much though he rages.
sentences.i: Yet he will not destroy you, however much he rages.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν δή is an emphatic denial, ‘surely not’. καταφθίσει is the future of καταφθίω ‘destroy utterly’. μάλα περ μενεαίνων has concessive περ, ‘though he rages hard’; μενεαίνω is the verb used of Poseidon’s anger at 1.20. Ino’s assurance matches what Zeus said at 1.74: Poseidon does not kill Odysseus, but drives him astray.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ὧδ’ ἔρξαι, δοκέεις δέ μοι οὐκ ἀπινύσσειν·
sentences.tr: alla mal’ hōd’ erxai, dokeeis de moi ouk apinyssein·
sentences.l: But do just this, and you seem to me not to lack sense:
sentences.i: But do just this, for you seem to me a man not lacking in sense:
sentences.n: ἔρξαι is the aorist infinitive of ἔρδω ‘do’, used as an imperative, a common Homeric way of giving instructions. ὧδε ‘thus’ points forward to what follows. δοκέεις is uncontracted (Attic δοκεῖς). ἀπινύσσειν is a rare verb, ‘be without understanding’, formed from ἀ- and the root of πινυτός ‘prudent’; οὐκ ἀπινύσσειν is understatement, ‘you are no fool’. The ano teleia serves as a colon before the instructions.

sentences.t:
εἵματα ταῦτ’ ἀποδὺς σχεδίην ἀνέμοισι φέρεσθαι
κάλλιπ’, ἀτὰρ χείρεσσι νέων ἐπιμαίεο νόστου
γαίης Φαιήκων, ὅθι τοι μοῖρ’ ἐστὶν ἀλύξαι.
sentences.tr:
heimata taut’ apodys schediēn anemoisi pheresthai
kallip’, atar cheiressi neōn epimaieo nostou
gaiēs Phaiēkōn, hothi toi moir’ estin alyxai.
sentences.l:
strip off these clothes, and the raft, to be carried by the winds,
leave behind, and swimming with your hands strive for a homecoming
to the land of the Phaeacians, where it is your fate to escape.
sentences.i: strip off these clothes and leave the raft for the winds to carry, and, swimming with your hands, strive for a homecoming to the land of the Phaeacians, where your portion is to escape.
sentences.n: ἀποδύς is the root aorist participle of ἀποδύω ‘strip off’. κάλλιπ’ is κατάλιπε ‘leave behind’, with κατα- cut short as in κάμμορε. φέρεσθαι is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to be carried’. χείρεσσι is ‘with your hands’, with the dative -εσσι. ἐπιμαίεο is an uncontracted imperative (Attic ἐπιμαίου), ‘strive for’, with the genitive νόστου, and γαίης Φαιήκων is the goal of that homecoming. μοῖρ’ ἐστίν is ‘it is your portion, your fate’, and ἀλύξαι ‘to escape’.

sentences.t:
τῆ δέ, τόδε κρήδεμνον ὑπὸ στέρνοιο τανύσσαι
ἄμβροτον·
sentences.tr:
tē de, tode krēdemnon hypo sternoio tanyssai
ambroton·
sentences.l:
Here, this head-veil beneath your chest stretch,
the deathless one;
sentences.i: Here, take this deathless head-veil and stretch it beneath your chest;
sentences.n: τῆ is an old word used while handing something over, ‘here, take’. τανύσσαι, the aorist infinitive of τανύω ‘stretch’, is again an infinitive for an imperative, with epic σσ. στέρνοιο has the genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου). κρήδεμνον, from κάρη ‘head’ and δέω ‘bind’, is a woman’s head-covering. ἄμβροτον ‘deathless’, from ἀ- and βροτός ‘mortal’, marks it as a thing of the gods, and it stands alone at the head of 347.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τί τοι παθέειν δέος οὐδ’ ἀπολέσθαι.
sentences.tr: oude ti toi patheein deos oud’ apolesthai.
sentences.l: and there is no fear for you of suffering anything, nor of perishing.
sentences.i: then you need have no fear of coming to any harm, or of being lost.
sentences.n: δέος ‘fear’ stands without ἐστί: ‘there is no fear’. παθέειν is an uncontracted aorist infinitive of πάσχω (Attic παθεῖν), and ἀπολέσθαι the aorist infinitive of ἀπόλλυμαι ‘perish’; both depend on δέος. τι is ‘anything’, the object of παθέειν, and τοι is ‘for you’. δέος here is less the feeling than the danger: there is nothing to fear.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν χείρεσσιν ἐφάψεαι ἠπείροιο,
ἂψ ἀπολυσάμενος βαλέειν εἰς οἴνοπα πόντον
πολλὸν ἀπ’ ἠπείρου, αὐτὸς δ’ ἀπονόσφι τραπέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autar epēn cheiressin ephapseai ēpeiroio,
aps apolysamenos baleein eis oinopa ponton
pollon ap’ ēpeirou, autos d’ aponosphi trapesthai.
sentences.l:
But when with your hands you lay hold of the dry land,
loosing it off, throw it back into the wine-faced open-sea,
far from the dry land, and yourself turn away apart.”
sentences.i: But when your hands have laid hold of the dry land, untie it and throw it back into the sea that has the look of wine, far out from the land, and turn yourself away.”
sentences.n: ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν ‘when’. ἐφάψεαι is an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel (Attic ἐφάψῃ), ‘lay hold of’, with the genitive ἠπείροιο; ἤπειρος is dry land as against sea. ἀπολυσάμενος is ‘having untied it from yourself’. βαλέειν and τραπέσθαι are infinitives for imperatives, and βαλέειν is uncontracted (Attic βαλεῖν). οἴνοπα πόντον keeps the house ‘wine-faced open-sea’. ἀπονόσφι is ‘away, apart’: he is not to watch the divine thing go back.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα θεὰ κρήδεμνον ἔδωκεν,
αὐτὴ δ’ ἂψ ἐς πόντον ἐδύσετο κυμαίνοντα
αἰθυίῃ ἐικυῖα·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsasa thea krēdemnon edōken,
autē d’ aps es ponton edyseto kymainonta
aithuiēi eikuia·
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the goddess gave him the head-veil, and she herself dived back into the sea as it swelled with waves, like a shearwater;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα keeps the house ‘So then having spoken’, here without elision. ἔδωκεν keeps its augment; Homer uses both forms. ἐδύσετο, like ἀνεδύσετο at 337, is an aorist of δύομαι with -σ- and thematic endings: she ‘dived’ where before she ‘rose’. κυμαίνοντα is ‘swelling with waves, surging’, from κῦμα. αἰθυίῃ ἐικυῖα repeats 337, and the bird-likeness frames her visit.

sentences.t: μέλαν δέ ἑ κῦμα κάλυψεν.
sentences.tr: melan de he kyma kalypsen.
sentences.l: and the dark wave covered her.
sentences.i: and the dark wave covered her.
sentences.n: ἑ is the old third-person pronoun, ‘her’ (it can also be ‘him’), used here as an enclitic, which is why δέ carries an accent. μέλαν is the neuter of μέλας ‘black, dark’, kept as ‘dark’ as in μέλας οἶνος ‘dark wine’. κάλυψεν is unaugmented, from καλύπτω ‘cover, hide’, the verb used of the clouds at 293.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ μερμήριξε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
autar ho mermērixe polytlas dios Odysseus,
ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l:
But he pondered, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
and, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: But much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus pondered, and, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: μερμήριξε is the aorist of μερμηρίζω ‘ponder, be of two minds’, without augment: he weighs whether to obey. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the house ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’, the name-formula that closes the line. Line 355 is word for word 298 and keeps its English: ὀχθήσας ‘vexed’, and the possessive ὃν … θυμόν, ‘his own heart’. His two speeches to himself frame Ino’s visit.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι ἐγώ, μή τίς μοι ὑφαίνῃσιν δόλον αὖτε
ἀθανάτων, ὅ τέ με σχεδίης ἀποβῆναι ἀνώγει.
sentences.tr:
ō moi egō, mē tis moi hyphainēisin dolon aute
athanatōn, ho te me schediēs apobēnai anōgei.
sentences.l:
“Oh me, I fear that someone is weaving a trick for me again,
one of the immortals, in that he bids me step off the raft.
sentences.i: “Oh me, I fear one of the immortals is weaving a trick for me yet again, in bidding me step off the raft.
sentences.n: ὤ μοι ἐγώ is the cry of 299 without δειλός; the nominative ἐγώ is part of the cry. μή with the subjunctive ὑφαίνῃσιν (epic -ῃσι) expresses a fear, ‘I fear that someone may be weaving’. δόλον ὑφαίνειν, ‘weave a trick’, is a craftsman’s image for plotting. ἀθανάτων, held over to 357, is partitive with τίς. ὅ τε is ‘in that, because’. ἀποβῆναι is ‘to step off’, with the genitive σχεδίης. ἀνώγει, a form of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, is present in sense.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ οὔ πω πείσομ’, ἐπεὶ ἑκὰς ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
γαῖαν ἐγὼν ἰδόμην, ὅθι μοι φάτο φύξιμον εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
alla mal’ ou pō peisom’, epei hekas ophthalmoisin
gaian egōn idomēn, hothi moi phato phyximon einai.
sentences.l:
But I will surely not obey yet, since far off with my eyes
I saw the land, where she said to me there was refuge.
sentences.i: No, I will not obey her yet, for the land where she told me I would find refuge was far off when I saw it with my eyes.
sentences.n: πείσομ’ is πείσομαι, here the future of πείθομαι ‘obey’; the future of πάσχω has the same form. οὔ πω is ‘not yet’. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν has the dative -οισι. ἐγών is ἐγώ in the form used before a vowel, and ἰδόμην is the unaugmented aorist middle of ὁράω, ‘I saw’. φάτο is ‘she said’, the unaugmented ἔφατο. φύξιμον is ‘a place of escape, refuge’, from φεύγω. He saw the mountains of the Phaeacians’ land at 279–281.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ὧδ’ ἔρξω, δοκέει δέ μοι εἶναι ἄριστον·
sentences.tr: alla mal’ hōd’ erxō, dokeei de moi einai ariston·
sentences.l: But I will do just this, and it seems to me to be best:
sentences.i: But this is what I will do, and it seems to me the best:
sentences.n: The line answers Ino’s ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ὧδ’ ἔρξαι at 342 with his own plan: ἔρξω is the future of ἔρδω ‘do’, where she used the infinitive as an imperative, and δοκέει δέ μοι takes up her δοκέεις δέ μοι. δοκέει is uncontracted (Attic δοκεῖ). εἶναι ἄριστον is ‘to be best’. The ano teleia again introduces what follows.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἂν μέν κεν δούρατ’ ἐν ἁρμονίῃσιν ἀρήρῃ,
τόφρ’ αὐτοῦ μενέω καὶ τλήσομαι ἄλγεα πάσχων·
sentences.tr:
ophr’ an men ken dourat’ en harmoniēisin arērēi,
tophr’ autou meneō kai tlēsomai algea paschōn·
sentences.l:
as long as the timbers hold fitted in their joinings,
so long I will stay right here and endure, suffering pains;
sentences.i: as long as the timbers hold together in their joinings, I will stay right here and endure, suffering pains;
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα is ‘as long as … so long’. The clause has both ἄν and κεν, a doubling Homer allows. δούρατ’ is δούρατα, the epic plural of δόρυ ‘beam, timber’. ἀρήρῃ is the perfect subjunctive of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, intransitive: ‘stay fitted’. ἁρμονίῃσιν, with -ῃσι, keeps ‘joinings’ from 248. αὐτοῦ is ‘right here’. μενέω is an uncontracted future (Attic μενῶ). τλήσομαι ‘I will endure’ shares its root with his epithet πολύτλας.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δή μοι σχεδίην διὰ κῦμα τινάξῃ,
νήξομ’, ἐπεὶ οὐ μέν τι πάρα προνοῆσαι ἄμεινον.
sentences.tr:
autar epēn dē moi schediēn dia kyma tinaxēi,
nēxom’, epei ou men ti para pronoēsai ameinon.
sentences.l:
but when the wave shakes the raft apart for me,
I will swim, since there is nothing better to think of beforehand.”
sentences.i: but when the wave shakes my raft apart, I will swim, since there is nothing better I can plan for.”
sentences.n: διὰ … τινάξῃ is tmesis for διατινάξῃ ‘shake apart’, an aorist subjunctive after ἐπήν ‘when’. μοι is ‘for me’, a dative of the person affected. νήξομ’ is νήξομαι, the future of νήχω ‘swim’. πάρα, with the accent drawn back, stands for πάρεστι ‘it is possible’. προνοῆσαι is ‘to think of beforehand’. His plan differs from Ino’s in one point: he will leave the raft when he has to, not before.

sentences.t:
ἧος ὁ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
ὦρσε δ’ ἐπὶ μέγα κῦμα Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων,
δεινόν τ’ ἀργαλέον τε, κατηρεφές, ἤλασε δ’ αὐτόν.
sentences.tr:
hēos ho tauth’ hōrmaine kata phrena kai kata thymon,
ōrse d’ epi mega kyma Poseidaōn enosichthōn,
deinon t’ argaleon te, katērephes, ēlase d’ auton.
sentences.l:
While he was pondering these things in mind and in heart,
roused up against him a great wave Poseidon the earth-shaker,
dread and grievous, roofed over, and struck him.
sentences.i: While he was turning this over in his mind and heart, Poseidon the earth-shaker roused a great wave against him, dread and grievous, roofing him over, and struck him with it.
sentences.n: Line 365 is word for word 4.120 and keeps its English there. ἧος is the epic form of ἕως ‘while’, and ὁ is ‘he’. ὥρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω ‘turn over, ponder’, with the augment lengthening ὁ- to ὠ-. ὦρσε δ’ ἐπί is tmesis for ἐπῶρσε ‘roused against’, aorist of ἐπόρνυμι. δεινόν τ’ ἀργαλέον τε keeps ‘dread and grievous’ from 5.175. κατηρεφές is ‘roofed over’, of a wave curling above him. The subject of ἤλασε may be Poseidon or the wave; ἔλασεν at 313 had the wave.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ἄνεμος ζαὴς ἠΐων θημῶνα τινάξῃ
καρφαλέων·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ anemos zaēs ēïōn thēmōna tinaxēi
karphaleōn·
sentences.l:
And as a hard-blowing wind shakes a heap of husks,
dry ones;
sentences.i: And as a hard-blowing wind shakes a heap of dry chaff,
sentences.n: A second simile, opened by ὡς δ’ ‘and as’ and closed by ὥς at 370. ζαής is ‘hard-blowing’, from the intensive ζα- and ἄημι ‘blow’. ἠΐων is the genitive plural of ἠΐα, here ‘husks, chaff’; a word of the same form means ‘provisions’. θημών is ‘heap’. τινάξῃ is an aorist subjunctive, as usual in a simile. καρφαλέων ‘dry, parched’ agrees with ἠΐων and is held over to 369, where the ano teleia follows it.

sentences.t: τὰ μὲν ἄρ τε διεσκέδασ’ ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ·
sentences.tr: ta men ar te dieskedas’ allydis allēi·
sentences.l: and it scatters them, then, one way and another;
sentences.i: and scatters them in all directions;
sentences.n: τά is ‘them’, the husks. διεσκέδασ’ is διεσκέδασε, the aorist of διασκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’; an aorist with epic τε states what always happens, the so-called gnomic aorist, which English renders by a present. ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ is ‘one way and another’, ἄλλυδις ‘to another place’ and ἄλλῃ ‘elsewhere’. The same verb returns in the next line, where the simile is applied.

sentences.t: ὣς τῆς δούρατα μακρὰ διεσκέδασ’.
sentences.tr: hōs tēs dourata makra dieskedas’.
sentences.l: so it scattered the long timbers of it.
sentences.i: so were the raft’s long timbers scattered.
sentences.n: ὥς ‘so’ applies the simile. τῆς is the pronoun, ‘of it’, the raft. δούρατα are the timbers Odysseus hoped would hold in their joinings at 361. διεσκέδασ’ repeats the verb of 369, now as a true past; its unstated subject is the wave, as the wind was in the simile. The sentence ends in mid-line, and the next begins with Odysseus.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἀμφ’ ἑνὶ δούρατι βαῖνε, κέληθ’ ὡς ἵππον ἐλαύνων,
εἵματα δ’ ἐξαπέδυνε, τά οἱ πόρε δῖα Καλυψώ.
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
amph’ heni dourati baine, kelēth’ hōs hippon elaunōn,
heimata d’ exapedyne, ta hoi pore dia Kalypsō.
sentences.l:
But Odysseus
went astride one timber, like one driving a riding-horse,
and stripped off the clothes which heavenly Calypso had given him.
sentences.i: But Odysseus got astride a single timber, like a man on a riding-horse, and stripped off the clothes which heavenly Calypso had given him.
sentences.n: ἀμφ’ ἑνὶ δούρατι βαῖνε is ‘went astride one timber’, ἀμφί ‘on both sides of’. βαῖνε is unaugmented. κέληθ’ is κέλητα, elided and roughened before the breathing of ὡς: a κέλης is a horse for riding, not one yoked to a chariot. ὡς standing after its word is ‘as, like’. ἐλαύνων is ‘driving, riding’. ἐξαπέδυνε, with two preverbs, is ‘stripped off’. The second half of 372 repeats 321 and keeps its English.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δὲ κρήδεμνον ὑπὸ στέρνοιο τάνυσσεν,
αὐτὸς δὲ πρηνὴς ἁλὶ κάππεσε, χεῖρε πετάσσας,
νηχέμεναι μεμαώς.
sentences.tr:
autika de krēdemnon hypo sternoio tanyssen,
autos de prēnēs hali kappese, cheire petassas,
nēchemenai memaōs.
sentences.l:
And at once he stretched the head-veil beneath his chest,
and himself headlong into the salt-sea fell, his two hands spreading,
eager to swim.
sentences.i: At once he stretched the head-veil beneath his chest and plunged headlong into the sea, spreading out his hands, eager to swim.
sentences.n: τάνυσσεν is the unaugmented aorist of τανύω, with epic σσ: he does as Ino bade at 346, in her own words. πρηνής is ‘face down, headlong’. ἁλί is the dative of ἅλς ‘salt-sea’. κάππεσε is κατέπεσε, with κατα- cut short and its τ assimilated. χεῖρε is a dual, ‘his two hands’. πετάσσας is ‘spreading’. νηχέμεναι, an infinitive in -έμεναι (Attic νήχειν), depends on μεμαώς, the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’.

sentences.t:
ἴδε δὲ κρείων ἐνοσίχθων,
κινήσας δὲ κάρη προτὶ ὃν μυθήσατο θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
ide de kreiōn enosichthōn,
kinēsas de karē proti hon mythēsato thymon·
sentences.l:
And the lord earth-shaker saw,
and, shaking his head, he spoke to his own heart:
sentences.i: And the lord earth-shaker saw him, and shaking his head he spoke to his own heart:
sentences.n: ἴδε is unaugmented, with the object ‘him’ understood. κρείων ἐνοσίχθων keeps the house ‘the lord earth-shaker’, Poseidon unnamed as at 282. Line 376 is word for word 285 and keeps its English: κάρη is the epic ‘head’, προτί is πρός, and ὃν … θυμόν is the possessive ‘his own heart’. He speaks to himself, but what he says is addressed to Odysseus in the second person.

sentences.t:
οὕτω νῦν κακὰ πολλὰ παθὼν ἀλόω κατὰ πόντον,
εἰς ὅ κεν ἀνθρώποισι διοτρεφέεσσι μιγήῃς.
sentences.tr:
houtō nyn kaka polla pathōn aloō kata ponton,
eis ho ken anthrōpoisi diotrepheessi migēēis.
sentences.l:
“So, now, having suffered many evils, wander over the open-sea,
until you mingle with Zeus-nurtured men.
sentences.i: “Wander over the sea like this, then, with the many evils you have suffered, until you come among Zeus-nurtured men.
sentences.n: οὕτω ‘thus, in this state’ is said with scorn. παθών is the aorist participle of πάσχω. ἀλόω is the present imperative of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’: ἀλάεο contracted to ἀλῶ, then drawn out again to ἀλόω. εἰς ὅ κεν is ‘until’, with κε (= ἄν) and the subjunctive μιγήῃς, an aorist passive of μίγνυμι with the vowel stretched (Attic μιγῇς): ‘mingle with, come among’. ἀνθρώποισι and διοτρεφέεσσι have the datives -οισι and -εσσι. διοτρεφής keeps the house ‘Zeus-nurtured’; the men are the Phaeacians.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὥς σε ἔολπα ὀνόσσεσθαι κακότητος.
sentences.tr: all’ oud’ hōs se eolpa onossesthai kakotētos.
sentences.l: But not even so do I expect you to make light of your evil.”
sentences.i: But even so, I do not expect you will think your evil a small thing.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὥς is ‘but not even so’: not even when he reaches the Phaeacians. ἔολπα is a perfect of ἔλπω with present sense, ‘I expect’. ὀνόσσεσθαι is a future infinitive of ὄνομαι ‘find fault with, scorn’; with the genitive κακότητος it is taken as ‘make light of’, think it too slight. The exact force is debated: either he will not be able to call his evil small, or, with grim irony, he will have no cause to complain of too little. The English keeps the first. κακότητος also ended Poseidon’s speech at 290.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἵμασεν καλλίτριχας ἵππους,
ἵκετο δ’ εἰς Αἰγάς, ὅθι οἱ κλυτὰ δώματ’ ἔασιν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas himasen kallitrichas hippous,
hiketo d’ eis Aigas, hothi hoi klyta dōmat’ easin.
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he lashed the fair-maned horses,
and came to Aegae, where his famous halls are.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and lashed the fair-maned horses, and came to Aegae, where his famous halls are.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας keeps the house ‘So then having spoken’. ἵμασεν is the aorist of ἱμάσσω ‘lash’, from ἱμάς ‘strap, thong’. καλλίτριχας ἵππους keeps ‘fair-maned horses’: the sea-god drives a team. ἵκετο is ‘came, reached’. Αἰγαί, a plural name, is a seat of Poseidon; which of several places so called is meant is not certain. οἱ is ‘his’. κλυτά is ‘famous’. ἔασιν is the epic εἰσί ‘are’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διὸς ἄλλ’ ἐνόησεν.
sentences.tr: autar Athēnaiē kourē Dios all’ enoēsen.
sentences.l: But Athena, daughter of Zeus, devised another thing.
sentences.i: But Athena, daughter of Zeus, thought of something else.
sentences.n: Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διός keeps the house ‘Athena, daughter of Zeus’; Ἀθηναίη is a longer epic form of Ἀθήνη. ἄλλ’ ἐνόησεν, ‘devised another thing’, uses the words of the fixed line ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη, and keeps their English. ἄλλ’ may be ἄλλο or ἄλλα. αὐτάρ ‘but’ sets her against Poseidon, who has just left the scene.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι τῶν ἄλλων ἀνέμων κατέδησε κελεύθους,
παύσασθαι δ’ ἐκέλευσε καὶ εὐνηθῆναι ἅπαντας·
sentences.tr:
ē toi tōn allōn anemōn katedēse keleuthous,
pausasthai d’ ekeleuse kai eunēthēnai hapantas·
sentences.l:
Truly she bound fast the paths of the other winds,
and bade them cease and go to rest, all of them;
sentences.i: She bound fast the paths of the other winds and ordered them all to cease and lie down to rest;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is ‘truly, indeed’. κατέδησε is the aorist of καταδέω ‘bind fast’: the winds’ paths are tied shut. κελεύθους, masculine beside the more usual neuter plural κέλευθα, is ‘paths’. τῶν ἄλλων ‘the other’ winds are all but the one she is about to send. παύσασθαι is ‘to stop’, and εὐνηθῆναι, an aorist passive of εὐνάω, ‘to lie down to rest’, as in a bed, εὐνή.

sentences.t:
ὦρσε δ’ ἐπὶ κραιπνὸν Βορέην, πρὸ δὲ κύματ’ ἔαξεν,
ἧος ὃ Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισι μιγείη
διογενὴς Ὀδυσεὺς θάνατον καὶ κῆρας ἀλύξας.
sentences.tr:
ōrse d’ epi kraipnon Boreēn, pro de kymat’ eaxen,
hēos ho Phaiēkessi philēretmoisi migeiē
diogenēs Odyseus thanaton kai kēras alyxas.
sentences.l:
and she roused up the rushing North Wind, and broke the waves ahead of him,
until he with the oar-loving Phaeacians should mingle,
Zeus-sprung Odysseus, death and the fates having escaped.
sentences.i: and she roused the rushing North Wind and broke the waves ahead of him, until Zeus-born Odysseus should come among the oar-loving Phaeacians, having escaped death and the fates of death.
sentences.n: ὦρσε δ’ ἐπί is tmesis again, ‘roused on’, as at 366, where Poseidon roused the wave. κραιπνός is ‘rushing’. πρὸ … ἔαξεν, with the verb that broke the mast at 316, is ‘broke the waves ahead of him’. ἧος with the optative μιγείη is ‘until he should mingle’, a purpose seen from the past. ὃ is the pronoun ‘he’, named in 387. Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισι has two long datives. Line 387 is word for word 2.352 and keeps its English; κῆρες are the fates of death.
